summaries.demographer: Fredick Burley is a 64-year-old African-American man born in Brooklyn, New York, and currently living alone in a rented apartment in Brooklyn 11204 (Q51, Q85-Q89). He has never been married, has no children, and maintains important kin ties with his sister Denise, niece Tasha, and nephew Marcus (Q05, Q84). His highest educational attainment is an associate's degree in business administration, and his life course reflects stable working-class to lower-middle-class mobility through long-term retail operations management and later consulting (Q90, Q65). His parents were Southern-born Great Migration migrants with high school educations who worked as a nursing aide and building maintenance worker (Q01, Q100-Q107).
summaries.behavioral_economist: Fredick is cautious, budget-conscious, and loss-averse, shaped by variable consulting income and memories of working-class discipline (Q56-Q64, Q83). He values flexibility and autonomy but responds to uncertainty by building spreadsheets, maintaining emergency savings, delaying discretionary purchases, and following up on invoices (Q60-Q62, Q81-Q82). His choices show strong preference for practical stability over prestige, visible in his late-twenties decision to stay in a local operations role rather than pursue a corporate track (Q02-Q04). He spends selectively on health, food, travel dreams, and hobbies, but cuts back quickly on restaurants, books, photo supplies, and tools when income tightens (Q60, Q81).
summaries.political_scientist: Fredick is a regular voter and moderately strong Democrat whose politics combine civil rights commitments, institutional skepticism, and a manager's concern for competent implementation (Q23-Q24, Q95-Q96). His views on race, policing, and Black Lives Matter are deeply informed by personal and generational experience with police scrutiny and Black urban history (Q20-Q30). He is civically engaged through voting, discussion, small donations, cultural attendance, and one local march rather than sustained organizational activism (Q23, Q29). He supports public services, health care access, worker dignity, fair policing, and small-business survival, while remaining wary of slogans without workable execution (Q24-Q25).
summaries.psychologist: Fredick presents as introverted, conscientious, reflective, and problem-focused, with a strong need for autonomy and order (Q01, Q11, Q43). He acknowledges anxiety expressed through overthinking, excessive list-making, repeated checking, and avoidance of stressful calls, but manages it through routine, walking, jazz, spreadsheets, and selective social support (Q43-Q45, Q50). His identity is organized around usefulness, dignity, memory, craft, and reliability, rather than status or social visibility (Q65, Q109). Relationally, he is private but attached: he avoids public vulnerability yet maintains steady family calls, a small friend circle, and mentoring relationships with younger workers (Q05-Q07, Q49, Q108).
